input:
Start-up

The pressure relief valve that is the subject of this chapter is an extremely important item of safety equipment, since it protects the equipment to which it is fitted against the potentially serious consequences of excessive pressure. Under normal circumstances the valve remains closed, but if the pressure within the protected equipment should rise to the set pressure, the valve will open automatically, allowing fluid to be discharged until such time as the pressure has fallen back to a more acceptable level, at which point the valve will close again. This chapter describes the procedures for the start-up, the normal operation, the alarm response, and the shutdown of the valve.

Prior to start-up, a thorough inspection of the valve and of the associated equipment should be carried out. The valve body, the inlet and outlet flanges, and the discharge line should be examined carefully for any evidence of damage, corrosion, or previous leakage. It should be confirmed that the discharge line is completely clear along the whole of its length and terminates at the designated safe discharge point, with no cap, plug, or closed valve situated anywhere along the path. Where an inlet isolation valve has been fitted, it should be verified that this valve is fully open and secured in the open position. The pressure gauge on the protected equipment should be checked to ensure that it is readable and has not become isolated from the equipment it serves. Any defects identified should be reported before pressurisation is commenced.

The pressure in the protected equipment should then be raised slowly, in accordance with the normal start-up procedure that applies to that particular equipment, and the pressure gauge should be observed closely while this is being done. As the normal operating pressure is approached and reached, it should be confirmed that the relief valve remains firmly shut, with no discharge at the outlet and no leakage at the flange joints. Once the equipment has settled down at its normal operating pressure, an entry should be made in the operating log recording that the valve is in service, that the inlet is open, and that the discharge path has been proved to be clear.

In the event that the valve is found to be leaking or discharging at normal operating pressure during the start-up, no attempt should be made to adjust it. The spring, the adjuster, and any seals on the valve should be left strictly alone. If the discharge continues, the pressure should be reduced, the supervisor should be informed, and the valve should be left for examination under a maintenance permit,.

Normal operation

During normal operation, the relief valve remains shut, and the protected equipment operates at a pressure below the set pressure of the valve

During each round, the valve and its joints should be inspected visually for leakage, corrosion, and mechanical damage, and the operator should listen out for any hissing sound that might indicate that the valve is passing. The discharge outlet should be examined for any discharge that should not be present, and also for deposits, staining, or icing that might indicate that a discharge has taken place at some point since the previous round. All findings should be recorded in the operating log, including quiet rounds, as evidence that the required watch has been kept.

The area in the vicinity of the valve and of the discharge outlet should be kept clear at all times. No materials should be stored against the discharge line, and nothing should be hung from the valve or from its associated pipework. The valve should not be painted, and particular care should be taken to avoid painting the spring housing or the nameplate, because paint applied to the moving and venting parts of a relief valve can trap moisture against the metal surfaces and can also conceal the corrosion that inspections are intended to detect.

There are three prohibitions that apply throughout the whole of normal operation. The inlet isolation valve should never be closed while the protected equipment remains pressurised, because an isolated valve protects nothing. The discharge outlet should never be plugged, capped, or blanked for any reason whatsoever, even where a passing valve is causing inconvenience. The set pressure should never be adjusted by the operator, because adjustment and bench testing are maintenance activities carried out under permit with the valve removed. Any valve that is passing, leaking at a joint, or showing signs of damage should be reported to the supervisor during the same shift, and the report should be entered in the operating log.

Alarms

There are two alarms on the protected equipment that are relevant to the relief valve, and the actions that are required in response to each of these alarms are described under the appropriate headings below. Neither alarm calls for work on the relief valve mechanism itself; the actions required are concerned instead with the pressure within the equipment and with the positioning of personnel in the area.

High pressure in the protected equipment

This alarm indicates that the pressure in the protected equipment has risen towards the set pressure, and that the relief valve may consequently be about to lift. Before any action is taken, the reading should be confirmed by reference to the local pressure gauge. The pressure should then be reduced by the normal means available for the equipment, which may involve cutting the feed, the heat input, or the inflow responsible for raising the pressure. Personnel should keep well clear of the discharge outlet, and if the pressure continues to rise, personnel should withdraw from the area in the vicinity of the discharge, the supervisor should be informed, and the valve should be allowed to perform its intended function. After the pressure has fallen and the valve has reseated, the event should be recorded in the operating log, and the valve should be reported for inspection.

Discharge at the relief valve outlet

This alarm indicates that the relief valve has lifted, or is passing heavily, with the result that fluid is being discharged. All personnel should keep well clear of the discharge outlet and of any area that the discharge can reach, and it should be confirmed, by reference to the pressure gauge, that the pressure within the protected equipment is falling. No attempt should be made to close, block, or throttle the discharge, and the valve should not be approached while a discharge is in progress. If the pressure is not falling, the supervisor should be informed immediately and the emergency procedure for the protected equipment should be followed. Once the discharge has stopped and the pressure is steady, the lift should be recorded in the operating log, together with the cause where this is known, and the valve should be reported for examination.

Shutdown

It should be borne in mind that the relief valve remains in service until such time as the protected equipment has been fully depressurised, and that the shutdown of the equipment does not in itself provide any justification for isolating the valve at an earlier stage. The valve continues to guard the equipment for as long as any pressure remains within it, including pressure that builds up again from heat or a leaking isolation.

The pressure should be reduced in accordance with the normal shutdown procedure for the protected equipment, and the pressure gauge should be monitored until the reading demonstrates that the equipment has been fully depressurised, a state that should be proved by the vent or drain before any isolation is touched. Only at this stage, and only where the valve is to be removed for bench testing or replacement, should the inlet isolation valve be closed. The drain or vent between the protected equipment and the valve should be opened, and it should be proved that no pressure remains trapped within the short length of pipe between the closed isolation and the valve before any attempt is made to loosen a flange bolt.

The removal of the valve is a maintenance activity and is carried out under permit, so that the part played by the operator is essentially that of the hand-over. An entry should be made in the operating log to the effect that the valve has been removed, identifying the equipment that it guarded and the state in which the equipment has been left, and any open flange left behind by the removal should be blanked Equipment from which the relief valve has been removed should not be repressurised until a valve has been restored to service on it, or an approved alternative protective arrangement is in place.

In summary, then, the valve guards pressurised equipment and is proved at start-up with its inlet open and its discharge path clear; during normal operation it is watched carefully and is otherwise left entirely alone; its two alarms call for the reduction of pressure and for the clearance of the discharge area; and it remains in service at shutdown until the protected equipment has been proved to be free of pressure.
target:
Start-up

A pressure relief valve guards the equipment it is fitted to against pressure above the limit the equipment is built to withstand. The valve opens when the pressure in the protected equipment reaches the set pressure, discharges fluid until the pressure has fallen, and closes again. This chapter covers start-up, normal operation, alarm response, and shutdown for the valve

Before start-up, walk round the valve and the protected equipment. Inspect the valve body, the inlet and outlet flanges, and the discharge line for damage, corrosion, and signs of past leakage. Confirm that the discharge line is clear along its whole run and ends at the safe discharge point, with no cap, plug, or closed valve in the path. Confirm that the inlet isolation valve, where one is fitted, is fully open and secured open. Check that the pressure gauge on the protected equipment is readable and is not isolated from the equipment it serves. Report any defect you find before the equipment is pressurised; a relief valve with a blocked discharge or a closed inlet gives no protection at all.

Raise the pressure in the protected equipment slowly, by the normal start-up procedure for that equipment. Watch the pressure gauge as the pressure rises. As the equipment reaches its normal operating pressure, confirm that the relief valve remains shut: no discharge at the outlet, no sound of passing fluid, and no leakage at the flange joints. Check each joint in turn and deal with any leak by the procedure for the protected equipment, not by work on the relief valve. When the equipment is steady at its normal operating pressure, record in the operating log that the valve is in service, the inlet is open, and the discharge path has been proved clear.

If the valve leaks or discharges at normal operating pressure during start-up, do not adjust it. Do not touch the spring, the adjuster, or any seal on the valve. Reduce the pressure if the discharge continues, inform the supervisor, and leave the valve for examination under a maintenance permit. A valve that cannot stay shut at normal pressure is not in service, whatever its position on the equipment.

Normal operation

In normal operation the relief valve is shut and the protected equipment runs below the set pressure. Your duty in this state is watchkeeping. The valve needs no adjustment, no operation, and no routine movement from you, and any interference with it reduces the protection it gives.

On each round, look at the valve and its joints for leakage, corrosion, and mechanical damage. Listen for the hiss that shows the valve is passing. Look at the discharge outlet for discharge that should not be there, and for deposits, staining, or icing that show discharge has taken place since the last round. Read the pressure gauge on the protected equipment and compare the reading with the normal operating band for the equipment. Record what you find in the operating log, including rounds on which nothing unusual is found: a log entry that shows a quiet round is evidence that the watch was kept.

Keep the area round the valve and the discharge outlet clear. Store no material against the discharge line, and hang nothing from the valve or its pipework. Protect the valve from knocks during lifting work and cleaning work nearby, and report any damage at once. Do not paint the valve, and in particular do not paint the spring housing or the nameplate. Paint on the moving and venting parts of a relief valve can hold moisture against the metal and can hide the corrosion that an inspection is meant to find.

Three prohibitions govern the whole of normal operation. Never close the inlet isolation valve while the protected equipment is pressurised; an isolated relief valve protects nothing. Never plug, cap, or blank the discharge outlet for any reason, including a passing valve that is making a nuisance of itself. Never adjust the set pressure; adjustment and bench testing belong to maintenance, under permit, with the valve off the equipment. A valve that passes, leaks at a joint, or shows damage is reported to the supervisor the same shift, and the report is entered in the operating log

Alarms

Two alarms on the protected equipment concern the relief valve. The action for each alarm is set out under its heading. No other alarm in this chapter calls for work on the relief valve itself, and in both cases your work is on the pressure and on people's positions, never on the valve mechanism.

High pressure in the protected equipment

Pressure in the protected equipment has risen towards the set pressure, and the relief valve may be about to lift. Confirm the reading on the local pressure gauge before acting on it. Reduce the pressure by the normal means for the equipment: cut the feed, the heat input, or the inflow that is raising the pressure, as the procedure for the equipment directs. Keep clear of the discharge outlet and keep other people clear of it. If the pressure continues to rise, withdraw from the area round the discharge, inform the supervisor, and let the valve do its work. When the pressure has fallen and the valve has reseated, record the event in the operating log and report the valve for inspection before the equipment is returned to unrestricted service.

Discharge at the relief valve outlet

The relief valve has lifted, or is passing heavily, and fluid is discharging. Keep yourself and all other personnel clear of the discharge outlet and of the area the discharge reaches. Confirm from the pressure gauge that the pressure in the protected equipment is falling. Do not attempt to close, block, or throttle the discharge, and do not approach the valve while it is discharging. If the pressure is not falling, inform the supervisor at once and follow the emergency procedure for the protected equipment. When the discharge has stopped and the pressure is steady, record the lift in the operating log, with the cause if it is known, and report the valve for examination; a valve that has lifted is inspected before its next period of service is relied on.

Shutdown

The relief valve stays in service until the protected equipment is fully depressurised. Shutdown of the equipment is not a reason to isolate the valve early: the valve guards the equipment for as long as any pressure remains in it, including pressure that builds up again from heat or from a leaking isolation after the main pressure source has been cut.

Reduce the pressure by the normal shutdown procedure for the protected equipment. Watch the pressure gauge until the reading shows that the equipment is fully depressurised, and prove the state by the vent or drain on the equipment before any isolation is touched. Only then, and only where the valve is to be removed for bench testing or replacement, close the inlet isolation valve. Open the drain or vent between the protected equipment and the valve, and prove that no pressure is trapped in the short length of pipe between the closed isolation and the valve before any flange bolt is loosened

Removal of the valve is a maintenance task and is done under permit. Your part is the hand-over: enter in the operating log that the valve has been removed, which equipment it guarded, and the state the equipment has been left in. Blank any open flange that removal leaves behind. Equipment from which the relief valve has been removed is not to be repressurised until a valve is back in service on it, or an alternative protective arrangement approved for the purpose is in place.

The chapter in restatement: the valve guards pressurised equipment and is proved at start-up with its inlet open and its discharge clear; in normal operation it is watched and left alone; its two alarms call for pressure reduction and for clearance of the discharge area; and it stays in service at shutdown until the equipment is proved free of pressure.
